blocks.text: Extrusion moulding is a continuous method for forming thermoplastics into products of uniform cross-section.
The diagram shows the wire-coating arrangement. The same screw-and-die principle produces pipes, rods and other continuous profiles with a suitable die.

blocks.title: Procedure
items: Feed polymer granules into a hopper above a heated barrel.
A rotating screw conveys, compresses and melts the material.
Force the melt through a die of the required cross-section.
Cool and solidify the extrudate, then pull it forward and cut or wind it.

blocks.text: Products: pipes, rods, sheets and wire insulation. Advantages include continuous production and high output; the cross-section is controlled by the die.

blocks.text: Extrusion produces continuous uniform-cross-section items and packaging film. The material is melted in a heated barrel and forced by a screw through a die, then cooled and collected.
The diagram shows the wire-coating arrangement. The same screw-and-die principle produces pipes, rods and other continuous profiles with a suitable die.
A flat die produces sheet/film; an annular die can produce a tube that is expanded and cooled to make blown film. For hollow packaging containers, blow moulding is used.

blocks.title: Blow-moulding steps
items: Make a hot polymer tube or preform.
Close the split mould around it.
Blow compressed air inside so the polymer expands against the mould wall.
Cool, open the mould and remove the hollow article.

blocks.text: Compression moulding shapes a measured polymer charge using heat and pressure in a mould. It is widely used for thermosetting resins and can also process some thermoplastics.

blocks.title: Procedure
items: Place the measured charge in the heated lower mould cavity.
Close the upper mould and apply pressure so the charge flows into the cavity.
Maintain heat and pressure until the thermoset cures; a thermoplastic is cooled sufficiently to set.
Open the mould, eject the article and trim flash.

blocks.text: Advantages: relatively simple tooling, good finish and suitability for large or thick parts. Limitations: slower cycles, flash and less suitability for very complex shapes. Applications: switches, plugs, handles and moulded trays.

questions.source_prompt: Explain the preparation properties and uses of Bakelite/phenol formaldehyde resin. [BL-1]

blocks.text: Bakelite is a thermosetting phenol–formaldehyde resin prepared by condensation polymerisation.

blocks.title: Preparation
items: Phenol reacts with formaldehyde at ortho and para positions to form hydroxymethyl phenols.
Condensation forms methylene bridges between phenolic rings, eliminating water.
Acid catalysis with limited formaldehyde gives novolac; curing with hexamethylenetetramine forms the cross-linked network.
Under suitable basic conditions, a resol intermediate can cure on heating to the three-dimensional thermoset.

blocks.text: Properties: hard, rigid, infusible after curing, heat-resistant and electrically insulating. Uses: switches, plugs, appliance handles, laminates and adhesives.

Further reactions at available ortho/para positions build a rigid three-dimensional network. Curing is irreversible: the finished resin cannot be melted and remoulded like a thermoplastic. The restricted chain motion gives dimensional stability, while electrical insulation and heat resistance suit electrical fittings and handles.

questions.prompt: Discuss the following properties of polymers crystallinity and glass transition temperatures. [BL-2]
questions.source_prompt: Discuss the following properties of polymers crystallinity and glass transition temperatures. [BL-2]

blocks.text: Crystallinity is the fraction of ordered regions formed by closely packed polymer chains. Most crystalline polymers also contain amorphous regions.

blocks.title: Factors affecting crystallinity
items: Regularity, symmetry and suitable stereochemistry favour packing.
Branching, irregular sequences and bulky side groups hinder packing.
Intermolecular forces and cooling/annealing conditions affect the ordered fraction.

blocks.text: Greater crystallinity generally increases density, stiffness and resistance to solvent penetration, while often reducing transparency and flexibility.
Glass transition is the change of the amorphous portion from glassy/rigid to rubbery/mobile as temperature rises through Tg. It differs from melting of crystalline regions.

blocks.title: Factors affecting Tg
items: Greater chain rigidity, strong intermolecular attraction and cross-linking usually raise Tg.
Plasticisers and increased chain flexibility generally lower Tg.
Increasing molecular weight raises Tg towards a limiting value.
Bulky groups that hinder rotation often raise Tg, though flexible side chains can have the opposite effect.
